title: New Site From Suffolk Law Dean Andrew Perlman Catalogs AI Policies at 128 Law Schools
author: Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: Ambrogi accepts the need to combine AI instruction with protected independent assessment and materially extends that proposition by documenting a broad policy pattern: schools restrict AI in graded work and exams, teach AI elsewhere, and redesign assessments to make student performance more observable. He also appropriately limits the strength of this evidence because the archive is incomplete and partly unverified.
qs: Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Ambrogi materially strengthens the synthesis with a source-linked inventory showing that many schools combine restrictions on assessed AI use with expanding instruction and assessment redesign. He also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that policy counts are incomplete snapshots, not evidence of educational effectiveness.
qs: Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

The site’s methodology section says that ChatGPT Sites was used extensively to research and construct the archive, with ChatGPT locating many of the public sources, organizing them into topic categories, and helping draft the summaries  Perlman, the site says, has not manually reviewed or independently confirmed every reference or summary, and readers should consult the linked original sources.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s selective-deployment and capability-development proposition into legal education. It documents a concrete institutional model that restricts unsupervised or unauthorized use while simultaneously expanding mandatory AI literacy, reinforcing the importance of use-context controls and trained users.
qs: Some schools treat unauthorized AI use as cheating, others as plagiarism, others as “unauthorized assistance.” But the basic rule is remarkably consistent, with schools such as Stanford, Northwestern, Virginia, Michigan (proposed for 2026-27), North Carolina, Wisconsin, and dozens of others all requiring some version of instructor opt-in.
- ** Mandatory AI instruction is spreading.**  Notably, even as law schools are restricting AI use, they are mandating its training.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between AI instruction and independent assessment by identifying a prevalent model of teaching AI while restricting it in graded work and exams. It also reinforces the cluster’s evidentiary caution: the policy inventory is AI-assisted, incomplete and not independently verified, so it cannot establish comprehensive prevalence or professional readiness.
qs: Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: Ambrogi supports the cluster’s core proposition by identifying a prevalent middle course: schools restrict AI in graded work and examinations while expanding AI instruction elsewhere. His evidence also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that policy inventories show varied responses rather than proving which educational approach works, because the archive is incomplete and selectively scoped.
qs: Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

kp.k: Archive maps legal education's varied AI responses
kp.d: Bob Ambrogi reports that Suffolk Law dean Andrew Perlman's archive catalogs public AI policies, teaching strategies and curricular programs at 128 of 196 U.S. law schools. The spreadsheet, current as of Aug. 2, 2026, contains 279 topic records across eight subjects. Entries link to schools' published documents and distinguish measures in effect from interim, pilot, proposed, guidance and completed/limited measures; the archive is comparative rather than a ranking.
qs: The spreadsheet I downloaded, current as of Aug. 2, 2026, contains 279 topic records spanning eight subjects at 128 law schools.
Each source is also labeled by its status: in effect, interim, pilot, proposed, guidance, or completed/limited.

kp.k: AI-assisted compilation limits completeness and verification
kp.d: The archive's methodology discloses extensive ChatGPT Sites use for research, categorization and summaries; Perlman has not independently confirmed every reference or summary. Ambrogi also used Claude to analyze the downloaded data. Coverage is limited to qualifying public sources: absence does not establish that a school lacks a policy, and generic university policies, individual syllabi, admissions-only rules and journal policies are excluded. These limitations qualify the reported counts and patterns.
qs: Perlman, the site says, has not manually reviewed or independently confirmed every reference or summary, and readers should consult the linked original sources.
The site notes that a school’s absence from a topic does not mean it lacks a policy, and schools governed by university-wide AI rules may not appear at all.
The inventory excludes generic university policies, individual syllabi, admissions-only rules, and journal policies.
Since Perlman used ChatGPT to create the site, I enlisted its competitor Claude to evaluate it.

kp.k: Instructor authorization governs AI use in assessed work
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that most of the 58 schools catalogued for submitted and graded work prohibit AI unless an instructor expressly authorizes it, usually in writing. Schools classify unauthorized use variously as cheating, plagiarism or unauthorized assistance. Nearly all 53 schools catalogued for exams similarly prohibit AI absent permission. These are findings about the archive's covered schools, including some proposed policies, rather than all U.S. law schools.
qs: With regard to AI use for submitted and graded work, of the 58 schools catalogued, the majority prohibit AI by default unless the instructor expressly authorizes it, usually in writing.
Some schools treat unauthorized AI use as cheating, others as plagiarism, others as “unauthorized assistance.”
The same is true for exams, with nearly all 53 catalogued schools prohibiting AI use during an examination absent instructor permission.

kp.k: Berkeley's breadth distinguishes otherwise typical default restrictions
kp.d: Ambrogi revises the framing of Berkeley's controversial policy: its instructor-opt-in structure resembles the majority approach, but he describes its scope as unique. It prohibits AI across stages from conceptualization to editing, limits permitted research to source identification and bans uploading course materials. Only Berkeley, St. Mary's and Suffolk appear in the archive's uploading category; Suffolk's July 27 memo proposes narrower restrictions on class recordings and identifiable student contributions uploaded without permission.
qs: Its basic structure, a default prohibition from which instructors can deviate in writing, is the majority approach.

That said, Berkeley’s policy is still unique for its breadth, in that it enumerates prohibited AI use at every stage from conceptualizing to editing, limits permitted research use to identifying sources, and bars students from uploading any course materials into AI systems.

kp.k: Mandatory AI education expands alongside use restrictions
kp.d: The article counts 26 schools with mandatory AI curriculum or literacy requirements, while its examples include both existing and forthcoming measures. Case Western Reserve's required first-year certification launched in February 2025; the school describes it as the first nationally of its kind. Mississippi College adopted the same requirement beginning the preceding spring. UC Law San Francisco will require an AI-enabled lawyering lab beginning with the Class of 2029, and UNLV adds a responsible-use course in fall 2026. Other models include Texas's three-year learning objectives, Ohio State's mandatory three-part first-year workshop series and AI instruction embedded in first-year skills courses.
qs: Twenty-six schools have mandatory AI curriculum or literacy requirements, and the list is growing semester by semester.

Case Western Reserve requires all first-year students to complete its Introduction to AI and the Law certification, launched in February 2025 and described by the school as the first required legal-AI certification of its kind nationally.
UC Law San Francisco will require every J.D. student, starting with the Class of 2029, to complete an AI-enabled lawyering lab.
Texas maps AI learning objectives across all three years of its J.D. program.
Ohio State runs a mandatory three-part AI workshop series for all 1Ls.

kp.k: Optional AI training broadens professional preparation
kp.d: The archive catalogs optional AI curriculum and opportunities at 66 schools, the largest topic category. Examples include certificates at Drake and Rutgers, a 12-credit concentration at St. Thomas (Minnesota), and forthcoming programs at Emory and Boston University in the 2026 academic year. Ambrogi interprets the combined curricular and policy findings as suggesting convergence toward restricting AI in assessments while teaching its use elsewhere, rather than demonstrating universal adoption.
qs: Sixty-six schools offer elective AI courses, certificates, concentrations, clinics or labs.
St. Thomas (Minnesota) offers a 12-credit AI concentration.
Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

kp.k: AI prompts secure and live assessment redesign
kp.d: Ambrogi identifies changes in how schools assess students, not just rules governing AI use. Texas reports near-elimination of take-home exams, more secure in-class exams and interest in participation, live presentations and oral examinations. Chicago is piloting device-free classrooms and no-access exam conditions across required first-year courses for 2026-27. Suffolk proposes interim secure summative assessment requirements in foundational courses. These examples have different implementation statuses and do not establish a sector-wide rate of change.
qs: Chicago is piloting device-free classrooms and no-access exam conditions across all of its required first-year courses for 2026-27.
Suffolk’s memo proposes interim requirements for secure summative assessments in foundational courses.

kp.k: Written course policies create instructor-specific compliance demands
kp.d: The archive identifies 20 schools requiring written disclosure of course-level AI policies, typically in syllabi. Wisconsin requires faculty to establish and communicate policies; Suffolk's interim measure for 2026-27 would require syllabi to distinguish permitted, prohibited and conditional uses. Ambrogi argues that students consequently must navigate instructor-by-instructor rules. Separately, the inventory catalogs faculty teaching guidance and support at 37 schools and AI use for studying and learning at 16.
qs: According to Perlman’s inventory, 20 schools have rules requiring instructors to disclose their course-level AI policies in writing, typically in the syllabus.
Suffolk’s interim measure for 2026-27 would require every syllabus to state what AI use is permitted, prohibited and conditional.
For law students, that means they will now have to be prepared to navigate a patchwork of instructor-by-instructor rules on using AI.

kp.k: Comparative policy evidence can inform institutional revision
kp.d: Ambrogi argues that, despite its provenance and coverage caveats, the archive provides more detailed understanding of legal education's AI response than scattered reporting or high-level surveys. He encourages schools with policies to contribute and suggests the archive as a starting point for schools drafting or revising policies; this is an editorial recommendation, not evidence of improved educational outcomes.
qs: Those caveats aside, the site clearly addresses a gap in understanding how legal education is responding to AI, providing greater detail than had been available through scattered news stories or high-level surveys.
For law schools that have policies, let us hope they will support and contribute to this effort.
For those that are in the process of drafting or revising their own policies, this may now be the first place to look.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi describes legal education as converging on restricted AI use in assessment alongside expanded AI instruction, with changes to assessment methods and course-policy disclosure.
pts.d: The claims concern legal education rather than legal-service pricing, employment or market structure. Ambrogi reports that default prohibitions, subject to instructor permission, predominate among catalogued policies for graded work and exams. He argues that Berkeley's default-prohibition structure is therefore less exceptional than its coverage suggested, although its restrictions remain unusually broad. He reports expanding mandatory and optional AI instruction, and changes toward secure, in-person or alternative assessments. He also claims that course-level policy disclosure requires students to navigate varying instructor rules. Separately, he presents Perlman's archive as filling an information gap for schools developing or revising policies.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is an AI-assisted inventory of published law-school documents, supplemented by named institutional examples; it is not a comprehensive or independently verified survey.
pts.d: Ambrogi bases his synthesis on Perlman's downloadable archive and uses Claude to help analyze it. The spreadsheet contains 279 topic records at 128 of 196 U.S. law schools. Reported category counts include 66 schools with optional AI opportunities, 58 with graded-work policies, 53 with exam policies, 26 with mandatory AI instruction, and 20 with course-policy disclosure rules. Assessment examples include Texas's reported near-elimination of take-home exams and greater use of secure in-class assessments, Chicago's pilot of device-free classrooms and no-access exam conditions, and Suffolk's proposed secure assessments. These examples and category counts support the author's descriptive synthesis; the article does not provide longitudinal totals quantifying the claimed semester-by-semester growth. Perlman's archive links to primary documents but was assembled extensively using ChatGPT, and not every reference or summary was manually verified.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe an August 2026 snapshot that mixes effective rules with proposals, pilots and future curriculum requirements.
pts.d: The dataset is current as of August 2, 2026. Examples of curricular expansion range from Case Western Reserve's February 2025 certification launch to fall 2026 courses and UC Law San Francisco's requirement beginning with the Class of 2029. Chicago's assessment pilot and Suffolk's proposed syllabus requirement concern 2026–27. Default AI prohibitions generally allow instructor-authorized exceptions. The archive labels policy status and excludes generic university policies, individual syllabi, admissions-only rules and journal policies; absence from a category does not establish absence of a policy. Consequently, the reported prevalence claims refer to catalogued schools and topics, not necessarily every U.S. law school.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are law students, faculty and law-school administrators.
pts.d: Students face restrictions on AI-assisted graded work and exams, mandatory or elective AI training, changing assessment formats and varying course-specific permissions. Some rules also restrict uploading course materials or identifiable student contributions to AI services. Faculty must establish and communicate AI policies and, in the cited initiatives, adapt teaching and assessment. Administrators can use the archive to compare institutional approaches and inform policy drafting or revision. The article does not establish downstream effects on lawyers' employment, clients or legal-service markets.
